newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland acts to defend Polish from English onslaught.
newsitem.headline: Poland acts to defend Polish from English onslaught.

text.p: Poland is drafting legislation to try to defend Polish from the onslaught of English and other foreign languages in official documents and advertising.
A cabinet committee this week approved a bill which would bring in fines where official instructions and guarantees on goods and advertisements were set out only in foreign languages.
"We Poles have a sense of danger emerging, not to the purity of Polish, but to the role of the language in various areas of life," said Walery Pisarek, one of the bill's authors.

"This is the worst danger a language can face -- not contamination by foreign words, but removal from various areas of law, agreements involving a Polish side, or computing," the linguistics professor told Reuters.

The Polish Language bill, also designed to replace a 1945 decree which took no account of linguistic minorities, aims to entrench Polish as the official language and to protect consumers buying imported products like drugs, ministerial adviser Kalina Kobelinska said.
She said a legislative committee would give an opinion and the government would then decide on sending it to parliament.
Many Poles worry that, with the boom in foreign contacts and trade since the 1989 collapse of communism, foreign languages are taking over business, science, popular culture and slang.
Documents, including agreements with foreigners, would now have to be in Polish as well as any other languages, Pisarek said.
Pisarek said fines proposed by the bill would not apply to borrowed expressions used in Polish, no matter how inelegant.
"It gives grounds for penalties only if Polish is absent, not if it is ugly," the Krakow-based professor said.
"There is nothing more dangerous than to give yourself the goal of linguistic purity. All languages ceaselessly undergo various influences," he added.

The bill does provide for creation of a Polish Language Council, which has already been formed, which could be approached for expert guidance on how words should be coined or adopted so as to preserve Polish spelling and grammar.
He said, for example, that established borrowings like "biznesmen" (businessmen) or the card game "brydz" (bridge) were sometimes reverting to their English spellings and this should be discouraged.

"But I can't imagine the council would have the same form as its equivalent in France which is backed by law and periodically issues lists of expressions to replace English words... which officials have to follow," he said.
